title: How do you handle late-arriving / out-of-order data in a streaming pipeline (event-time vs processing-time, watermarks, allowed lateness, windowing), and how do you reprocess historical data (replay from Kafka/object store, backfill jobs, idempotent/exactly-once writes)?
shortTitle: Handling late / out-of-order data and reprocessing in a streaming pipeline

s1_definition.profdef: Late and out-of-order data is handled by computing on event-time rather than processing-time, using watermarks to estimate how far event-time has progressed, windows to bucket events by when they happened, and an allowed-lateness period to still admit stragglers before finalizing a window. Reprocessing historical data is handled by replaying events from the durable log or object store into backfill jobs, with idempotent or exactly-once writes so re-running never duplicates or corrupts results.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India tallies card spend minute by minute, but some slips arrive late from a branch with poor network. Processing-time tallying would wrongly count a 10:00 slip in the 10:05 minute just because it arrived late. Event-time tallying reads the real time stamped on the slip and files it in the correct minute. A watermark is the supervisor saying "I'm now fairly sure all slips up to 10:03 have arrived." Allowed lateness is a short grace period to still accept a straggler from 10:02. And if the bank later finds a mistake, it re-feeds the stored slips through the counter again — and because each slip is filed by its unique id, re-running fixes totals without double-counting.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use event-time with watermarks and allowed lateness for correct windows despite stragglers, and reprocess by replaying with idempotent writes so re-runs never duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Late and out-of-order data is handled by computing on event-time rather than processing-time, using watermarks to estimate how far event-time has progressed, windows to bucket events by when they happened, and an allowed-lateness period to still admit stragglers before finalizing a window. Reprocessing historical data is handled by replaying events from the durable log or object store into backfill jobs, with idempotent or exactly-once writes so re-running never duplicates or corrupts results.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India tallies card spend minute by minute, but some slips arrive late from a branch with poor network. Processing-time tallying would wrongly count a 10:00 slip in the 10:05 minute just because it arrived late. Event-time tallying reads the real time stamped on the slip and files it in the correct minute. A watermark is the supervisor saying "I'm now fairly sure all slips up to 10:03 have arrived." Allowed lateness is a short grace period to still accept a straggler from 10:02. And if the bank later finds a mistake, it re-feeds the stored slips through the counter again — and because each slip is filed by its unique id, re-running fixes totals without double-counting.

**One line to remember:** Use event-time with watermarks and allowed lateness for correct windows despite stragglers, and reprocess by replaying with idempotent writes so re-runs never duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is distinguishing event-time from processing-time. Event-time is when the event actually happened, carried inside the record, while processing-time is when the engine happens to see it. In the real world events are delayed and arrive out of order because of network hiccups, retries, and mobile devices going offline, so computing per-minute aggregates on processing-time produces wrong buckets. Correct streaming uses event-time, so a transaction stamped 10:00:30 is counted in the 10:00 minute even if it arrives at 10:04.

Because event-time streams never cleanly "end" a time period, engines use watermarks. A watermark is a moving marker that flows with the stream and asserts "I believe I have now seen all events with event-time up to T." It is usually derived as the maximum observed event-time minus a bounded-lateness allowance. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the engine can fire and finalize that window's result. You configure allowed lateness, a grace period after the watermark during which a straggler can still update an already-fired window, after which very late events are dropped or routed to a side output for separate handling. In Flink this reads like `stream.assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))).keyBy(Txn::getAccountId).window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1))).allowedLateness(Time.seconds(30))`, declaring five seconds of expected disorder and thirty seconds of lateness grace.

Windowing is how you bound an infinite stream into finite computations. Tumbling windows are fixed, non-overlapping buckets like each one-minute interval; sliding windows overlap, like a one-minute window every ten seconds; and session windows group bursts separated by gaps. All of them key off event-time so late data lands in the right window.

Reprocessing historical data is the other half. Because the durable log (Kafka) and the lake (object store) retain events, you reprocess by replaying from a chosen offset or re-reading stored Parquet, then running a backfill job to recompute results for a past period. The critical requirement is that reprocessing must be safe, which means idempotent or exactly-once writes. Idempotency is achieved with upserts keyed by a stable event id, so replaying the same events overwrites rather than duplicates. Exactly-once is achieved with transactional sinks plus checkpointed offsets, so a failure and restart neither lose nor double-apply events. A senior nuance is to keep windowing logic deterministic and to version your transformations, so a backfill run months later reproduces consistent results, which in a bank is essential because corrected figures may feed regulatory resubmissions and must be reproducible and auditable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Card events arrive out of order, so a 10:00 swipe may land after a 10:01 swipe. Counting by arrival would corrupt per-minute totals. This is exactly event-time windowing — bucket by the real event time.

Problem 2 — We must decide when a minute is "done" despite stragglers. This is exactly a watermark plus allowed lateness — finalize when the watermark passes, but still accept a brief straggler.

Problem 3 — A mistake is found and we must recompute without double-counting. This is exactly replay plus idempotent writes keyed by event id.

The mini-project models this. `CardEvent` carries an event-time. `EventTimeWindower` assigns each event to its one-minute event-time window, tracks a watermark as max-seen-time minus a lateness bound, finalizes windows when the watermark passes, and admits late events within allowed lateness while dropping very late ones. `IdempotentStore` stores window results by key for replay-safety. The demo feeds out-of-order events plus a late straggler and then replays to prove idempotency.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four of Rajesh's card events arriving out of order by event-time, with 60-second windows, a 5-second watermark lag, and 30 seconds of allowed lateness.

Step 1 — E1 arrives (event-time 30). It falls in the 0-to-60 window, which gets a running total of 1200. The watermark advances to 30 minus 5, which is 25.

Step 2 — E2 arrives (event-time 10). Even though it arrived after E1, its event-time places it in the same 0-to-60 window, so the total becomes 2000. This is event-time correctness: arrival order did not matter.

Step 3 — E3 arrives (event-time 95). It belongs to the 60-to-120 window and pushes the watermark to 95 minus 5, which is 90. Because 90 is past the end of the 0-to-60 window, that window is finalized and stored with total 2000.

Step 4 — E4 arrives late (event-time 45). It belongs to the already-finalized 0-to-60 window, but the watermark 90 is still within the 60-plus-30 allowed-lateness boundary of 90, so it is admitted rather than dropped, demonstrating allowed lateness accepting a straggler.

Step 5 — Replay proves idempotency. The whole stream is reprocessed. Because the store upserts by account-and-window key, finalized windows overwrite themselves rather than duplicating, so the store size stays the same after the replay. Out-of-order data was handled by event-time windows and watermarks, and reprocessing was safe because writes were idempotent.

```
INFO: === RUN 1 (out-of-order + late straggler) ===
INFO: WINDOW[0-60] SAV2001 += 1200 (eventId E1, watermark 25)
INFO: WINDOW[0-60] SAV2001 += 800 (eventId E2, watermark 25)
INFO: WINDOW[60-120] SAV2001 += 500 (eventId E3, watermark 90)
INFO: STORE SAV2001|0 = 2000
INFO: WINDOW[0-60] SAV2001 += 300 (eventId E4, watermark 90)
INFO: STORE SAV2001|60 = 500
INFO: Store size after run 1 = 2
INFO: === REPLAY (reprocessing, must be idempotent) ===
INFO: Store size after replay = 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Events arrive OUT OF ORDER (by event-time)
  arrival: E1(t=30) E2(t=10) E3(t=95) E4(t=45,late)
    │ assign to window by EVENT-TIME (not arrival)
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ window[0-60):   E1(1200)+E2(800)+E4(300 late) │
  │ window[60-120): E3(500)                        │
  └───────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                  │ watermark = maxSeen - 5
                  │ finalize window when watermark ≥ windowEnd
                  │ allowedLateness=30 admits E4
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ IdempotentStore (upsert key) │  ← replay-safe
  │ SAV2001|0 = 2000             │
  │ SAV2001|60 = 500             │
  └──────────────────────────────┘
  replay → same 2 keys overwrite → no duplication
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I handle late and out-of-order data by computing on event-time instead of processing-time. Event-time is when the event actually happened, carried in the record, whereas processing-time is just when the engine saw it, and because real-world events are delayed and arrive out of order, aggregating on processing-time would put them in the wrong buckets. To decide when a time period is complete despite stragglers, I use watermarks, which are moving markers derived from the maximum observed event-time minus a bounded-lateness allowance that assert the stream has probably seen everything up to a given time. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the engine finalizes it, and I configure allowed lateness as a grace period during which a straggler can still update an already-fired window, after which very late events are dropped or routed to a side output. Windows themselves bound the infinite stream, whether tumbling, sliding, or session, and they all key off event-time so late data lands correctly.

Reprocessing historical data is the other half. Because the durable log and the lake retain events, I replay from a chosen offset or re-read stored Parquet and run a backfill job to recompute a past period. The non-negotiable requirement is that reprocessing is safe, which I achieve with idempotent writes using upserts keyed by a stable event id, or with exactly-once using transactional sinks and checkpointed offsets, so re-running neither loses nor double-applies events. I also keep the windowing logic deterministic and version my transformations so a backfill months later reproduces consistent results.

In my project at the National Bank of India this mattered for per-minute card-spend aggregates. Swipes arrived out of order and sometimes late from branches with poor connectivity, so I bucketed them by event-time, used a watermark to finalize each minute, and allowed a short lateness window to still admit stragglers. When a calculation error was found, I replayed the stored events through a backfill job, and because every write was an idempotent upsert keyed by account and window, the corrected totals came out right without any double-counting. That reproducibility and safety is essential in a bank because corrected figures can feed regulatory resubmissions and must be auditable.
